# Connected reductive groups over infinite fields are generated by finitely many tori

`Langlands.GroupScheme.ReductiveFiniteTorusGenerationStatement` states that,
for every infinite field `k : Type u` and every actual group scheme `G` over
`Spec k` with `IsConnectedReductive G`, there are a natural number `m`, group
schemes `T j` over `Spec k` (`j : Fin m`) and homomorphisms `ι j : T j ⟶ G`
such that

1. every `T j` is a torus (`IsTorus (T j)`);
2. every `ι j` is a closed subgroup (`IsClosedSubgroup (ι j)`, that is,
   `(ι j).hom.hom.left` is a closed immersion);
3. the `ι j` generate `G`: for every group scheme `H` over `Spec k` and every
   closed subgroup `i : H ⟶ G` such that each `ι j` factors through `i` as a
   morphism of `k`-schemes (`FactorsThrough (ι j).hom.hom i`, that is, there
   is `g : (T j).X ⟶ H.X` with `g ≫ i.hom.hom = (ι j).hom.hom`), the subgroup
   functor `SubgroupFunctor.range i` is all of `G`.

## Conventions

`GroupScheme (Spec (CommRingCat.of k))` is the category of group objects in
`Over (Spec k)`. `IsConnectedReductive G` (Reductive/Basic.lean) says that
`G.X` is smooth and affine over `Spec k`, that its underlying space is
connected, and that the base change of `G` to `AlgebraicClosure k` has trivial
unipotent radical (`HasTrivialUnipotentRadical`). Smoothness gives local finite
presentation, and affineness gives quasi-compactness, so `G` is of finite type
over `k`; smoothness also gives geometric reducedness. Thus `G` is a connected
group variety in Milne's sense (the note after Proposition 1.22, printed p.12,
PDF p.28). Milne 6.45–6.46 (printed p.135, PDF p.151) defines unipotence by
fixed vectors in representations and reductivity by triviality of the
geometric unipotent radical, matching the existing predicates: every smooth,
connected, normal, unipotent closed subgroup after base change to
`AlgebraicClosure k` has trivial range.

`IsTorus` (Torus/Lattice.lean) says that after base change to some field
extension `K : Type u`, the group is isomorphic to a finite product of copies
of `𝔾_m`. This is Milne's Definition 12.14 (printed p.236, PDF p.252).
The finite index type in `IsSplitTorus` can be empty. Neither this predicate
nor the statement requires the torus to split over `k`.

A closed subgroup `i : H ⟶ G` in the sense of `IsClosedSubgroup` identifies
`H` with a closed subgroup scheme of `G`. These are exactly Milne's algebraic
subgroups: Definition 1.3 (printed p.7, PDF p.23) defines an algebraic
subgroup as a `k`-subscheme `H` of `G` with an algebraic group structure for
which the inclusion is a homomorphism, and Proposition 1.41 (printed p.18,
PDF p.34) shows that algebraic subgroups are closed. The condition that `ι j`
factors through `i` says that `T j` is contained in `H`, which is Milne's
"`φ_i` factors through `H`" in Proposition 2.51.

`SubgroupFunctor.range i = ⊤` says that for every `k`-scheme `U`, every
`U`-point of `G` is the image of a `U`-point of `H`. Because `i` is a closed
immersion, and hence a monomorphism, this holds exactly when `i` is an
isomorphism, that is, when `H = G`. So condition 3 says that `G` is the
smallest algebraic subgroup of `G` containing all the `T j`: in Milne's
terminology (Proposition 2.51), the family `(ι j)` generates `G`.

The statement covers every infinite field, including imperfect ones, every
connected reductive group, split or not, and every universe `u`. No maximal
torus is supplied as a hypothesis. When `G` is trivial (the absolute rank-zero
case), `m = 0` is allowed. Then condition 3 holds because every point of `G`
is the identity, which lies in every subgroup.

Condition 2 is part of the conclusion because consumers need the tori to be
affine. The Library's `PointedImageGenerationStatement` requires an affine
source, and closed subgroups of the affine group `G` are affine (Milne,
Corollary 1.43,
printed p.19, PDF p.35). Without condition 2 this would have to be obtained by
descending affineness along a field extension, which Mathlib does not
provide.

## Provenance

The statement is derived content. Milne does not state it in this form. It
combines his Theorem 17.91 and Corollary 17.84 with a finiteness argument
from Section 2.h. The source is J. S. Milne, *Algebraic Groups* (2017),
registered as `milne-2017-algebraic-groups`. Printed page numbers equal PDF
page numbers minus 16. The registered errata snapshot
`milne-2017-algebraic-groups-errata-2026-11-02` was read in full. Its entry for
printed p.18 corrects the proof of Lemma 1.40, whose statement is retained;
it gives no correction to Proposition 1.41. The corrections to 1.45
(printed p.20) and Example 17.42 (printed p.364) do not affect this
derivation. There are no entries correcting 2.50–2.53, 17.43–17.44, 17.84
or 17.91.

1. Theorem 17.91 (printed p.381, PDF p.397): every connected group variety is
   generated by its Cartan subgroups. Milne proves this for infinite `k` and
   omits the finite case (Borel–Springer 1968, 2.9). This is the reason for
   the hypothesis `Infinite k`. "Generated" is meant in the sense of
   Proposition 2.51 (printed p.56, PDF p.72): `G` is the smallest algebraic
   subgroup through which all inclusions of Cartan subgroups factor.
2. Definition 17.43 and Proposition 17.44 (printed p.364, PDF p.380; recalled
   on printed p.381): the Cartan subgroups of `G` are the centralizers
   `C_G(T)` of the maximal tori `T` of `G`, and they are smooth and connected.
   Corollary 17.84 (printed p.379, PDF p.395): in a reductive group, a torus
   `T` is maximal if and only if `C_G(T) = T`. So the Cartan subgroups of a
   connected reductive group are exactly its maximal tori. They are tori over
   `k` and algebraic subgroups of `G`, hence closed subgroups (1.41).
3. Finitely many suffice. By Summary 1.36 (printed p.17, PDF p.33) a
   connected algebraic group is geometrically connected. For a finite family
   `C_1, …, C_r` of Cartan subgroups, consider the multiplication map
   `μ : C_1 × ⋯ × C_r → G`, `(c_1, …, c_r) ↦ c_1 ⋯ c_r`. Its source is
   geometrically reduced and geometrically connected, and its image contains
   `e`. An algebraic subgroup contains every `C_i` exactly when `μ` factors
   through it: multiply the factorizations in one direction, and put `e` in
   all coordinates but one in the other. So by Proposition 2.50
   (printed pp.55–56, PDF pp.71–72) the smallest algebraic subgroup
   `H_F` containing the `C_i` exists and is smooth, and by Proposition 2.53
   (printed p.56, PDF p.72) it is connected. (Only the statements of 2.50
   and 2.53 are used, not the sentence in the printed proof of 2.50 that
   `φⁿ` is dominant for large `n`.) Enlarging the family enlarges `H_F`. Its
   dimension is at most `dim G`. Include the empty family, whose generated
   subgroup is trivial; the set of these dimensions is therefore nonempty
   and bounded in `ℕ`. Choose a finite family `F` for which `dim H_F` is
   maximal. For any further Cartan subgroup `C`, the group
   `H_{F ∪ {C}}` is smooth and connected, contains `H_F` and has the same
   dimension. A closed irreducible subset of an irreducible variety of the
   same dimension is everything, and both groups are reduced, so they are
   equal. Thus `C ⊆ H_F`. Hence `H_F` contains every Cartan subgroup, and by
   item 1, `H_F = G`.

Taking for `T j` the members of `F` (with `m = |F|`) and for `ι j` their
inclusions gives conditions 1 and 2 by item 2. Condition 3 holds because
`H_F = G` is the smallest algebraic subgroup containing the `T j`, so any
closed subgroup `H` containing them contains `G`.

This module records the proposition only and supplies no proof. It is the
structural input for
`Langlands.GroupScheme.ReductiveTorusDominationStatement`: applying
`PointedImageGenerationStatement` to the ordered product of the `ι j` on the
product torus gives a closed subgroup containing every `T j` that is
dominated by a power of that ordered product. By condition 3 this subgroup is
all of `G`.
